Issued at 243 AM MDT Fri Aug 28 2026

230AM water vapor imagery shows an upper level high over the 
southwest CONUS with it's associated ridge axis extending over 
eastern Wyoming. This ridge has been positioned over western Wyoming 
the past few days, keeping convection largely diurnally driven and 
the temperatures hot and above normal. This will not be the case 
these next few days as Wyoming will be on the upstream side of the 
ridge in moisture rich southwest flow. A vorticity maximum with 
accompanying Pacific moisture is on track to reach west and 
northwest Wyoming around sunrise this morning. This vorticity 
maximum will be present across northwest portions of the state 
throughout the day. This means a rainy day is in store for locations 
such as Jackson Hole, Yellowstone National Park, and portions of the 
Bighorn Basin. Yellowstone looks to get the most rain today, with 12-
hour (6AM-6PM) rain totals upwards to 0.5" forecast. That being 
said, a few strong showers and embedded thunderstorms could 
producing moderate to heavy rainfall at times with localized 
flooding possible. Temperatures across these areas are forecast to 
be in the 60s to mid 70s due to dense cloud cover and 700mb 
temperatures of 6C to 8C. This vorticity maximum looks to shift 
north out of the area after 6PM, allowing for shower chances to drop 
to around 20% through 9PM/10PM tonight.

By early afternoon, shower and thunderstorm chances increase 
elsewhere as a weaker disturbance passes overhead. Low level 
moisture is not as abundant compared to northwest and northern 
portions, so convection is expected to initiate off the higher 
terrain of central and southwest Wyoming and trek northeast. There 
is generally a 20% to 40% chance of showers and thunderstorms for 
most areas between noon and 7PM. A few thunderstorms could produce 
gusty 45 to 50 mph winds due to dew point depressions around 45 
degrees. Temperatures across southern and central Wyoming will be 
quite a bit warmer compared to northwest parts of the state with 
highs in the 80s. These warmer temperatures can be attributed to 
700mb temperatures of 12C to 14C degrees. 

By late tonight, shower and thunderstorm chances begin to increase 
across western Wyoming as a shortwave approaches the area. This 
shortwave is forecast to have more abundant moisture with widespread 
PWATs above the 98th percentile of climatology from late 
tonight through midday Saturday. In addition to the abundant 
moisture, the shortwave will also provide support for a cold 
front to pass across the state. This front will focus the shower
and thunderstorm chances (60% to 90%) across western Wyoming 
early Saturday morning through the early afternoon before 
pushing east in the afternoon and evening (30% to 80% chances 
elsewhere). Winds will also be stronger across the Wind 
Corridor Saturday afternoon with the presence of a 60kt jet 
aloft and a tightening pressure gradient ahead of the front. 
Widespread wind gusts of 30 to 45 mph are forecast in and around
the Wind Corridor on Saturday afternoon.

The shower and thunderstorm chances increase once again on Sunday, 
especially across western and southern Wyoming, as a more potent 
cold front treks across the state. This cold front is associated 
with the eastward progression of a Pacific Northwest upper low 
into Montana. Most areas have a 40% to 90% chance of showers and
thunderstorms from midnight Saturday night through Sunday 
afternoon. All in all, there is high confidence in a rainy 
Friday through Sunday. From Friday afternoon through Sunday 
afternoon, there is a 70% to 90% chance of at least 1 inch of 
rain across west and northwest Wyoming, with the higher chances 
over the higher elevations. Across southwest and southern 
Wyoming, the 48-hour rainfall totals will not be as high with 
only a 50% to 70% chance of 0.5" of rain. Central and northern 
Wyoming will likely see only a few tenths, at best, during this 
timeframe. Widespread windy conditions are also forecast with 
this system on Sunday, with most locations seeing wind gusts of 
30 to 40 mph. Drier and cooler air quickly filters in behind the
front Sunday evening.

Monday morning is expected to be the coldest we have experienced in 
awhile, especially west of the Continental Divide. Across the 
western mountains, the western valleys, Yellowstone National Park, 
and the Upper Green River Basin, there is a 40% to 90% chance of 
Monday mornings lows being 35 degrees or less. However, temperatures 
are forecast to warm up into the upper 60s to 70s by Monday 
afternoon across those areas as a transitory ridge moves overhead.

Thursday on the position of an upper high. One model guidance 
positions a high over the southeast CONUS, which puts the 
Intermountain West in strong southwest flow with shortwaves
